questions.q: What will be the magnitude of the electric field at point $O$ as shown in the figure? Each side of the figure is $l$ and perpendicular to the other?
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let the point $O$ be the origin $(0,0)$ of a Cartesian coordinate system.

The positions and magnitudes of the charges are: $q_B = +q$ at $(-l, 0)$, $q_G = +2q$ at $(l, 0)$, $q_F = +q$ at $(0, -l)$, $q_A = -q$ at $(-l, l)$, $q_D = +q$ at $(l, l)$, $q_E = +2q$ at $(-l, -l)$, and $q_H = -q$ at $(l, -l)$.

Let $E_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{l^2}$.

The electric field contributions at the origin from the charges on the axes are:
$\vec{E}_B = E_0 \hat{i}$
$\vec{E}_G = -2E_0 \hat{i}$
$\vec{E}_F = E_0 \hat{j}$

The net electric field from these axial charges is:
$\vec{E}_{axial} = \vec{E}_B + \vec{E}_G + \vec{E}_F = -E_0 \hat{i} + E_0 \hat{j}$

The distance of all corner charges from the origin is $\sqrt{l^2 + l^2} = l\sqrt{2}$. The electric field contributions at the origin from the corner charges are:
$\vec{E}_A = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{(l\sqrt{2})^2} \left( \dfrac{-\hat{i} + \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} (-\hat{i} + \hat{j})$
$\vec{E}_D = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{(l\sqrt{2})^2} \left( \dfrac{-\hat{i} - \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} (-\hat{i} - \hat{j})$
$\vec{E}_E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{2q}{(l\sqrt{2})^2} \left( \dfrac{\hat{i} + \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \dfrac{2E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} (\hat{i} + \hat{j})$
$\vec{E}_H = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{(l\sqrt{2})^2} \left( \dfrac{\hat{i} - \hat{j}}{\sqrt{2}} \right) = \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} (\hat{i} - \hat{j})$

The net electric field from the diagonal charges is:
$\vec{E}_{diag} = \vec{E}_A + \vec{E}_D + \vec{E}_E + \vec{E}_H$
$\vec{E}_{diag} = \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} [ (-\hat{i} + \hat{j}) + (-\hat{i} - \hat{j}) + 2(\hat{i} + \hat{j}) + (\hat{i} - \hat{j}) ]$
$\vec{E}_{diag} = \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} [ (-1 - 1 + 2 + 1)\hat{i} + (1 - 1 + 2 - 1)\hat{j} ] = \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} (\hat{i} + \hat{j})$

The total electric field at the origin is $\vec{E}_{net} = \vec{E}_{axial} + \vec{E}_{diag}$:
$\vec{E}_{net} = (-E_0 \hat{i} + E_0 \hat{j}) + \dfrac{E_0}{2\sqrt{2}} (\hat{i} + \hat{j}) = E_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} - 1 \right) \hat{i} + E_0 \left( \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} + 1 \right) \hat{j}$

The magnitude of the net electric field is:
$|\vec{E}_{net}| = E_0 \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} - 1 \right)^2 + \left( \dfrac{1}{2\sqrt{2}} + 1 \right)^2 }$
$|\vec{E}_{net}| = E_0 \sqrt{ \left( \dfrac{1}{8} - \dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} + 1 \right) + \left( \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{2}{2\sqrt{2}} + 1 \right) }$
$|\vec{E}_{net}| = E_0 \sqrt{ \dfrac{2}{8} + 2 } = E_0 \sqrt{ 2.25 }$
$|\vec{E}_{net}| = 1.5 E_0 = \dfrac{3}{2} E_0$

Substituting $E_0 = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{l^2}$ back into the expression:
$|\vec{E}_{net}| = \dfrac{3}{2} \left( $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{l^2} \right)

questions.q:
Electric potential at a point& $P$~due to a point charge of $5 \times {10}^{- 9}C$ is $50V$. The distance of $P$ from the point charge is:
(Assume, $\dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}} = 9 \times {10}^{9}Nm^{2}C^{- 2}$)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The electric potential for a point charge is given by&

$V = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}r}$

The data given is~

$V = 50VQ = 5 \times {10}^{- 9}C$

So, the distance of the point~is~

~$r = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{Q}{V}$
$⇒ r = 9 \times {10}^{9} \times \dfrac{5 \times {10}^{- 9}}{50}$
$⇒ r = 0 . 9m = 90cm$

A very small point like piece of it of mass $m$ gets detached from the bottom of the sphere and falls down vertically under gravity. This piece carries charge $q$. If it acquires a speed $ν$ when it has fallen through a vertical height $y$ (see figure), then (assume the remaining portion to be spherical)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
$By using total energy conservation
$\Delta KE + ( \Delta PE{)}_{electo} + ( \Delta PE{)}_{gravitation} = 0$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mV^{2} + \left(k\dfrac{Qq}{R + y} - k\dfrac{Qq}{R}\right) + ( - mgy ) = 0$

$\dfrac{1}{2}mV^{2} = mgy + kQq\left(\dfrac{1}{R} - \dfrac{1}{R + y}\right); V^{2} = 2gy + \dfrac{2kQq}{m}\dfrac{y}{R ( R + y )}$

$V^{2} = 2y \left[\dfrac{qQ}{4\pi{ε}_{0}R ( R + y ) m} +g\right]$

$

questions.q: The electric field due to a short electric dipole at a large distance  \left(r\right)$& from center of dipole on the equatorial plane varies with distance as :$
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
An& electric dipole is a system of two charges of equal and opposite magnitude placed at a short distance.

The dipole moment is,& $p = 2ql$.

The electric field due to the dipole is,

$E = \dfrac{2kp}{r3}$

Clearly, the electric field varies as~$\dfrac{1}{r3}$.

questions.q: Two uniformly charged spherical conductors $A$~and $B$ of radii $5$ mm and $10$ mm are separated by a distance of $2$ cm. If the spheres are connected by a conducting wire, then in equilibrium condition, the ratio of the magnitudes of the electric fields at the surface of the sphere $A$ and $B$ will be
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
When two conductors& are connected by a conducting wire, their potentials become equal. Therefore,& ${V}_{A} = {V}_{B}$

The potential of a spherical conductor is given by,~$V = \dfrac{kQ}{R}$

$⇒ \dfrac{k{Q}_{A}}{RA} = \dfrac{k{Q}_{B}}{RB}$

$⇒ Q ∝ R$

Now the electric field near the surface of the conductor will be,~$E = \dfrac{kQ}{R2}$

$⇒ \dfrac{EA}{EB} = \dfrac{k{Q}_{A}{R}_A^{2}}{k{Q}_{B}{R}_B^{2}} = \dfrac{RB}{RA}$

$⇒ \dfrac{EA}{EB} = \dfrac{10}{5} = \dfrac{2}{1}$

questions.q: Let $\sigma$ be the uniform surface charge density of two infinite thin plane sheets shown in figure. Then the electric fields in three different region ${E}_{I}, {E}_{II}$ and~${E}_{III}$
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Electric field due to charged sheet for charge density& $+ \sigma$~is~$\overset{→}{E} = \dfrac{+ \sigma}{2{∈}_{0}}$~and for~$- \sigma$~is~$\overset{→}{E} = \dfrac{- \sigma}{2{∈}_{0}}$.

Assuming RHS to be $\overset{^}{n}$

$\overset{→}{E}I = \dfrac{σ}{2{∈}_{0}}\left(- \overset{^}{n}\right) + \dfrac{σ}{2{∈}_{0}}\left(- \overset{^}{n}\right) = - \dfrac{σ}{\in 0}\overset{^}{n}$~ (leftwards)

$\overset{→}{E}II = \dfrac{σ}{2{∈}_{0}}\left(- \overset{^}{n}\right) + \dfrac{σ}{2{∈}_{0}}\left(\overset{^}{n}\right) = 0$

$\overset{→}{E}III = \dfrac{σ}{2{∈}_{0}}\left(\overset{^}{n}\right) + \dfrac{σ}{2{∈}_{0}} \left(\overset{^}{n}\right) = \dfrac{σ}{\in 0}\left(\overset{^}{n}\right)& & (rightwards)

$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
For net force on charge placed at origin is given as&
$⇒ \dfrac{K{Q . q}^{ }}{\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)2} + \dfrac{KQ^{2}}{d2} = 0$, where~$K$~is a constant.

Solving the above equation, we get,~$q = \dfrac{- Q}{4}$

Hence, the charge~$q = - \dfrac{Q}{4}$~such that net force on the charge~$+ Q$& placed at origin is zero.

questions.q: A two point charges $4q$ and $– q$ are fixed on the $x$ -axis at $x = \dfrac{- d}{2}$ and $x = \dfrac{d}{2}$, respectively. If the third point charge ‘$q$ ’ is taken from the origin to $x = d$ along the semicircle as shown in the figure, the energy of the charge will:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Potential at origin& $O$, the potential due to two charges is given by

${V}_{0} = \dfrac{4q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right)} + \left(- q\right)4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = \dfrac{6q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}d}$

Potential at~$P$~at a distance,~$x = d$~is given by

${V}_{P} = \dfrac{4q}{4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{3d}{2}\right)} + \left(- q\right)4\pi{ε}_{0}\left(\dfrac{d}{2}\right) = \dfrac{q}{6\pi{ε}_{0}d}$

Change in potential energy due the charge motion of charge~$q$~is given by

~$∆ U = q\Delta V = q \left({V}_{f} - {V}_{i}\right)$

$⇒ ∆ U = q \left({V}_{P} - {V}_{O}\right)

$∆ U = $q\left(\dfrac{q}{6\pi{ε}_{0}d} - \dfrac{3q}{2\pi{ε}_{0}d}\right) = - \dfrac{4q^{2}}{3\pi{ε}_{0}d}

$

questions.q: A point charge& ${q}_{1} = 4{q}_{0}$ is placed at origin. Another point charge~${q}_{2} = - {q}_{0}$ is placed at $x = 12cm$. Charge of proton is ${q}_{0}$. The proton is placed on $x$-axis so that the electrostatic force on the proton in zero. In this situation, the position of the proton from the origin is ______~$cm$.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let at point& $P$~net electric field is zero.

As direction of electric field due to both charges at~point~$P$~is opposite, equating magnitude we get

$\dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{4{q}_{0}}{x2} = \dfrac{1}{4\pi{ε}_{0}}\dfrac{q0}{\left(x - 12\right)2} ⇒ 2\left(x - 12\right) = x ⇒ x = 24cm$

Distance of proton from origin $= 24cm$.

questions.q: $27$ identical drops are charged at $22V$ each. They combine to form a bigger drop. The potential of the bigger drop will be _____ $V$.
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Total volume of the drop will remain unchanged,

So, $27 \times \left(\dfrac{4}{3}\pir^{3}\right) = \dfrac{4}{3}\piR^{3}$

$⇒ R = 3r$

Potential of the small drops,~$22 = \dfrac{kq}{r}$

For bigger drop, potential will be

$V = k\left(27q\right)\left(3r\right) = 9\left(\dfrac{kq}{r}\right) = 9 \times 22 = 198V$
